summary: The specifications leave the route preference of IPv4 and IPv6 Extended Reachability TLVs unstated, and the effect of the up/down bit in Level 2 LSPs is inconsistent. This standards-track RFC defines the preference rules clearly so implementations choose routes consistently. It updates RFC 5308.

eli5.summary: When two roads lead to the same place, which should you take? This writes down a clear rule so all routers choose the same one.

questions: what is the is-is up/down bit
how does is-is choose between l1 and l2 routes
what does rfc 7775 change in rfc 5308
why did is-is routes loop between vendors
subtitle: A clear ranking of IS-IS routes learned from IPv4 and IPv6 extended reachability, and a fix for how the up/down bit is treated in Level 2.

tldr.problem: The route preferences for the IPv4 and IPv6 Extended Reachability TLVs were never stated explicitly, and the use of the up/down bit in Level 2 LSPs was inconsistent between RFCs, so different vendors chose different routes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the route types each TLV can carry, says the up/down bit is ignored (treated as 0) in Level 2 LSPs, and defines three preference groups: Level 1 internal and external routes first, then Level 2 and L1->L2 routes, then routes leaked downward or between instances at Level 1.
tldr.outcome: Implementations can choose routes the same way, which avoids the routing loop shown in the appendix. It updates RFC 5308 and corrects its IPv6 rule to match IPv4.

today: RFC 7775 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2016. It updates RFC 5308 and has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why Route Preference Needed Fixing
sections.content:
RFC 5302 defines route preference rules for TLVs 128 and 130. RFC 5305 introduced the IP Extended Reachability TLV 135 but did not explicitly adapt those rules. RFC 5308 defined the IPv6 Reachability TLV 236 and did state a preference, but in a way that uses the up/down bit in Level 2 LSPs, which is inconsistent with RFC 5302 and RFC 5305.

This RFC defines explicit rules for TLV 135, revises the rules for TLV 236 and clarifies the up/down bit in Level 2 TLVs. It is a clarification (not a correction) of RFC 5302 and RFC 5305, and a correction of RFC 5308 so that IPv6 matches IPv4. The same rules apply to the Multi-Topology (MT) TLVs 235 and 237.
sections.eli5: Older rulebooks left a gap and one of them said something different from the others. This new page fills the gap and makes them all agree.

sections.title: The Up/Down Bit in Level 2 LSPs
sections.content:
The up/down bit exists so that prefixes can be leaked downwards in the IS-IS level hierarchy. A route leaked downwards has the bit set to 1, and such prefixes MUST NOT be leaked upwards. With a single IS-IS instance and the current two levels, a prefix in a Level 2 LSP cannot have the bit set to 1. RFC 5302 still allowed for it in case a future extension added more levels, and recommended that implementations ignore the bit in L2 LSPs and accept the prefixes either way.

RFC 5305 added the case of several virtual routers in different areas redistributing prefixes between IS-IS instances. For a prefix advertised from one area to another at the same level, the bit SHALL be set to 1. It did not change the rule that the bit is ignored in Level 2 LSPs.

The conclusion is that there is no "L2 inter-area route". RFC 5308 nevertheless introduced one by giving a preference to a "Level 2 down prefix". This RFC calls that an error and corrects it. Because the change may cause interoperability issues, implementors may wish to support transition mechanisms from the RFC 5308 behavior.
sections.eli5: A little flag on a route says which way it came down the ladder. At the top rung the flag should be ignored, but one rulebook forgot that, and this page fixes it.

sections.title: Route Types Carried by the Extended Reachability TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 5302 remains the authority for TLVs 128 and 130. TLVs 135, 235, 236 and 237 do not support the internal/external metric distinction, and the IPv4 TLVs (135 and 235) do not distinguish internal from external routes. The Prefix Attribute Flags sub-TLV from a separate work-in-progress document brings that distinction back, using an X-Flag and an R-Flag.

For IPv4 (TLVs 135 and 235) the RFC defines these route types: L1 intra-area, L1 external, L2 intra-area, L1->L2 inter-area, L2->L2 inter-area, L2 external, L2->L1 inter-area and L1->L1 inter-area. For example, L1->L2 inter-area routes are advertised in L2 LSPs with the up/down bit 0, while L2->L1 inter-area routes are advertised in L1 LSPs with the bit set to 1. An L2->L2 inter-area route has the bit set to 1, but it is ignored and treated as if it were 0.

For IPv6 (TLVs 236 and 237) the same kinds of routes appear, with an external bit set to 0 or 1 and two extra types: L1->L2 external and L2->L1 external. Again, the L2->L2 inter-area route carries up/down 1 but it is ignored and treated as 0.
sections.eli5: Every route comes with a label saying where it started and where it has been, such as local, from far away, or passed along from another network. The rules list every kind of label.

sections.title: The Order of Preference
sections.content:
Routes of the same kind listed together are treated equally. For IPv4 routes in TLVs 135 or 235 the order is:

  1. L1 intra-area routes and L1 external routes.
  2. L2 intra-area routes, L2 external routes, L1->L2 inter-area routes and L2->L2 inter-area routes.
  3. L2->L1 inter-area routes and L1->L1 inter-area routes.

For IPv6 routes in TLVs 236 or 237 the order is the same, with the L1->L2 external routes added to the second group and the L2->L1 external routes added to the third.

Since L2->L2 inter-area routes are treated as if the up/down bit were 0, they sit in the same group as ordinary Level 2 routes, not in a separate lower group.
sections.eli5: There are three piles of routes. Always choose from the first pile that has something in it, then the second, then the third.

sections.title: A Real Routing Loop Example
sections.content:
Appendix A documents an interoperability issue caused by vendors reading the up/down bit in Level 2 LSPs differently. Two routers, R0 and R4, advertise the prefix 10/8. Router R3 runs two Level 2 IS-IS instances to split the network into two areas, and leaks prefixes from R4 into the other instance, setting the down bit as RFC 5305 specifies. R1, R2 and R3 are from three different vendors.

R0 advertises 10/8 with metric 2000 and R3 with metric 100, and all links have metric 1. R2 prefers the route that does not have the up/down bit set, so it picks R1 as next hop. R1 compares metrics (2001 versus 102) and picks R2. Each sends traffic to the other, and packets loop.
sections.eli5: Two friends use different rules to choose a path. One thinks the path goes through the other, and the other thinks the same back. They keep handing the ball back and forth.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it raises no new security considerations. Security considerations for the IS-IS protocol are covered in ISO 10589, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about here. The safety rules from the older documents still apply.
